title: When Was Deuteronomy Written? Major Scholarly Views
subtitle: Moses' law, a later narrative frame, and the evidence behind competing dates
summary: Deuteronomy attributes law to Moses but also narrates his death and looks back on earlier events. Many critical reconstructions connect a legal core with late-monarchic Judah and later editing, while traditional defenders argue for substantial Mosaic material with limited additions. The final book, its older contents, and a discovered law scroll must not be assigned the same date without argument.

seo.metaTitle: When Was Deuteronomy Written? Major Scholarly Views
seo.metaDescription: Moses' law, Josiah's scroll, later framing, and the critical and conservative arguments about Deuteronomy's date.

sections.title: Ask Which Part Is Being Dated
sections.body:
'When was Deuteronomy written?' can mean the age of its laws, the composition of its speeches, or the final narrative frame. Those need not have one date.

The strongest critical case is cumulative: retrospective narration, the centralization of worship, and the relationship with the law book in Josiah's reign. It supports substantial later shaping more directly than it proves the exact year or author of every passage.

sections.title: A Book That Speaks Through Moses
sections.body:
Deuteronomy presents Moses addressing Israel before entry into the land. Its central concern is loyalty to God and a covenantal way of life. Jewish and Christian tradition connects the work with Moses; modern critical models often see later writers transmitting and reshaping Mosaic tradition.

The difference is not whether the book is ancient or religiously serious. It is how directly its present words can be assigned to Moses and what later composition would mean for its authority.

sections.title: The Writing Notices and the Narrative Frame
sections.body:
Deuteronomy 31:9 and 31:24–26 attribute the writing of 'this law' to Moses. They do not explicitly tell us that he wrote every sentence of the finished book. The notices themselves are narrated, and chapter 34 recounts his death.

This observation is not a modern discovery designed to attack Judaism. [Bava Batra 15a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.15a?with=Talmud) preserves disagreement over the final verses. Traditional readers can allow an inspired addition or a special account of dictation without abandoning Mosaic law. The death narrative alone cannot date the whole legal core.

sections.title: Why Late-Monarchic and Exilic Settings Are Proposed
sections.body:
Deuteronomy 12:5 centers worship at the place God will choose. Second Kings 22:8–13 describes a law book discovered in the Temple under Josiah; the reforms that follow resemble important Deuteronomic concerns. Many scholars connect the texts and place a major legal form in that late-monarchic setting.

The [Catholic introduction](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/deuteronomy/0) also identifies later editing and a longer compositional history. These are inferences from the book and its context, not the discovery of a manuscript bearing a seventh-century author's signature. Different layers and models remain disputed.

sections.title: The Strongest Reply: Rediscovery Is Not Composition
sections.body:
Second Kings describes finding a law book, not writing it for the first time. An older law could become newly important in Josiah's reform. Also, Deuteronomy's chosen sanctuary is not named Jerusalem. These are serious cautions against turning a contextual fit into an exact composition date.

Treaty parallels are debated as well: [Aaron Koller's discussion](https://bibleinterp.arizona.edu/articles/2014/09/kol388003) explains why similarities across a long Near Eastern tradition complicate dating. The critical response appeals to the combined evidence, not centralization or treaty form alone. A substantial Mosaic core remains a defended position, though not the usual critical reconstruction.

sections.title: What a Muslim Can Conclude Without Overclaiming
sections.body:
Islam affirms God's revelation to Moses. It need not identify every sentence of the present Pentateuch with that original revelation. A later frame or substantial editing therefore matters to claims of direct wording, but it does not mean all Mosaic teaching vanished.

Quran 15:9 states the protection claim for the Quran, and 25:32 addresses its gradual delivery. Their truth is not established by a later date for Deuteronomy. The Quran's positive evidence must be examined separately, just as conservative Jewish and Christian evidence deserves an answer rather than a label.

sections.title: Why This Dating Question Matters
sections.body:
The case points toward distinguishing old tradition from the finished book, with genuine debate about the extent and date of editing. It does not justify calling every line a deliberate forgery or declaring one reconstruction certain.

Read [How Was the Bible Transmitted?](/articles/how-was-the-bible-transmitted) to keep composition separate from later copying. For the Islamic alternative, read [Written Compilation of the Quran](/articles/written-compilation-of-the-quran), comparing the actual evidence rather than two slogans.

bibleVerses.text: Moses wrote this law, and delivered it to the priests the sons of Levi, who bore the ark of Yahweh’s covenant, and to all the elders of Israel.

When Moses had finished writing the words of this law in a book, until they were finished, Moses commanded the Levites, who bore the ark of Yahweh’s covenant, saying, “Take this book of the law, and put it by the side of the ark of Yahweh your God’s covenant, that it may be there for a witness against you.

So Moses the servant of Yahweh died there in the land of Moab, according to Yahweh’s word. He buried him in the valley in the land of Moab opposite Beth Peor, but no man knows where his tomb is to this day.
Since then, there has not arisen a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom Yahweh knew face to face,
These are the words which Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan in the wilderness, in the Arabah over against Suf, between Paran, Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and Dizahab.
Jair the son of Manasseh took all the region of Argob, to the border of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and called them, even Bashan, after his own name, Havvoth Jair, to this day.)
But to the place which Yahweh your God shall choose out of all your tribes, to put his name there, you shall seek his habitation, and there you shall come.
In the eighteenth year of king Josiah, the king sent Shaphan, the son of Azaliah the son of Meshullam, the scribe, to Yahweh’s house, saying,

Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the scribe, “I have found the book of the law in Yahweh’s house.” Hilkiah delivered the book to Shaphan, and he read it. Shaphan the scribe came to the king, and brought the king word again, and said, “Your servants have emptied out the money that was found in the house, and have delivered it into the hands of the workmen who have the oversight of Yahweh’s house.” Shaphan the scribe told the king, saying, “Hilkiah the priest has delivered a book to me.” Then Shaphan read it before the king. When the king had heard the words of the book of the law, he tore his clothes. The king commanded Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam the son of Shaphan, Achbor the son of Micaiah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the king’s servant, saying, “Go inquire of Yahweh for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found; for great is Yahweh’s wrath that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not listened to the words of this book, to do according to all that which is written concerning us.”

The king commanded all the people, saying, “Keep the Passover to Yahweh your God, as it is written in this book of the covenant.” Surely there was not kept such a Passover from the days of the judges who judged Israel, nor in all the days of the kings of Israel, nor of the kings of Judah; but in the eighteenth year of king Josiah, this Passover was kept to Yahweh in Jerusalem.
Abram passed through the land to the place of Shechem, to the oak of Moreh. At that time, Canaanites were in the land.
Abraham called the name of that place Yahweh Will Provide. As it is said to this day, “On Yahweh’s mountain, it will be provided.”

(For only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of the Rephaim. Behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron. Isn’t it in Rabbah of the children of Ammon? Nine cubits was its length, and four cubits its width, after the cubit of a man.)

faq.question: Did Moses write 'this law' according to Deuteronomy?
faq.answer: Yes, the book attributes a body of law to him. Scholars dispute how much of the finished work that expression covers; the narrative frame is a separate question.

faq.question: Does the account of Moses' death prove all the laws are late?
faq.answer: No. It shows why the completed book requires explanation beyond ordinary autobiographical writing. It does not by itself date every earlier component.

faq.question: Was Josiah's scroll certainly the whole present book?
faq.answer: No. Many scholars connect it with Deuteronomy or a legal core, but the identification and extent are inferred. Second Kings describes a discovery, not an explicit composition.

faq.question: Do treaty similarities settle the date?
faq.answer: Not alone. Scholars dispute which parallels imply dependence and which reflect longstanding conventions. They must be considered with internal and historical evidence.

faq.question: Does a later final form make the book worthless?
faq.answer: No. It can preserve earlier law and religious testimony. The implications for revelation depend on the tradition's actual doctrine of inspiration and the extent of the evidence.

furtherReading.title: Bava Batra 15a
furtherReading.author: Babylonian Talmud; William Davidson edition
furtherReading.note: The traditional discussion includes different accounts of the Torah's final verses; it does not establish a modern date for the whole book.

furtherReading.title: Introduction to the Hebrew Bible
furtherReading.author: John J. Collins
furtherReading.note: Standard university textbook; its chapter on Deuteronomy summarizes the mainstream dating, the link to Josiah’s reform, and the Assyrian treaty parallels.

furtherReading.author: Kenneth A. Kitchen
